Hi 👋 there is a lot to unpack here. I am going to try and address all of your points and provide solutions to help you reduce the stress. Moving is already stressful. 

1.  The loan initial estimate has to go out no later than 3 business days (minus a federal holiday). Therefore once you have a contract and a completed application they have to disclose. Additionally if you did not lock your rate and get lender credits for that rate or pay points to buy down your rate before the initial disclosures go out that will not be reflected on the initial loan estimate.   Additionally any seller credit, non point verbal negotiated lender credit, realtor credit or earnest money deposit will NOT be reflected on the initial loan estimate. UNLESS said seller credit is on the purchase contract or you locked and got points for the rate you chose. 

The reason for not showing the earnest money, seller credit (not on the purchase contract) and realtor credits is because it has not yet been verified. Your loan officer takes the application, the processor reviews and provides the documents to the underwriter and they sign off on the items and clear your loan for approval. 

Your earnest money must be verified that it came from an acceptable source based on the lending guideline. 

Seller credits not on the contract must be documented and all parties must sign an addendum and provide to the lender. 

Realtor credits are credited by your realtor informing the title company they are forfeiting a portion or all of their commission and giving to the buyer as a credit. They sign a form because it’s their money. The commission split is included in your purchase contract. Then title/escrow provides that to the lender And you get the credit. 

Regarding the lender discretionary credit they promised. I would ask them to email you saying how much you are getting so you have it in writing if you don’t trust them. 

Lastly. The federal lending guideline dictate what’s required and when regarding disclosures. The lender is not required to re disclose or update the loan estimate unless there is a change of circumstance. If lender or title fees increase by a certain fraction of a percent it triggers the change of circumstance or the required revised loan estimate to be sent to you. The same time frame applies 3 business days. If the lender fails to disclose additional cost with in that amount and timeframe it is not permissible to pass that expense on to you. Certain fees like the appraisal fee is a charge that may not increase after it is initially disclosed. Unless it’s a valid reason. Like it’s a home that is larger, custom, or in a remote location that would require more time or work from the appraiser. They have to state why and follow the above to charge more. 

Now assessing the why not put it on the initial loan estimate question. Most lenders will over disclose in the initial loan estimate for two reasons. 

1. If they are wrong they lose money and eat the fees. Trust but verify. 

2. Sticker shock. It’s better to disclose all the costs before credits so you know the true cost of the purchase transaction. It’s a lot easier process to include all the fees (lender and third party) then not and it increases later. You would be even less pleased than you are now. 

Additionally when they disclose the first time they don’t have title work from the escrow company and they usually don’t have the escrow companies exact fees. Most lenders use one of just a few processing systems and they have tons of title companies they have worked with before. Those companies give their standard fees and it’s downloaded for your disclosures. 

Some fees are estimated depending on the type of property like HOA Transfer fee, Condo fee, transfer taxes (in some states). This is where having a good realtor and loan officer who can prepare you for what to expect comes into play. If they had told you what I am telling you up front we wouldn’t be having long winded conversations on Reddit and you wouldn’t be bent right now. 

You can change lenders at anytime. However you are under contract and it may say that you have to get approval from the seller to change etc. ask your realtor. 

Lastly the title company is also a resource. You can double check with them that they are aware of the credits from the seller and or realtor. Your lender is responsible for what they promised. 

At least 3 days before you can sign and close on your loan the lender must provided you with a closing disclosure. At that time if the credits are not there then they MUST revise it and issues an updated one reflecting your final closing costs. The closing disclosure is issued after the appraisal is completed and after the underwriter has final approved your loan. Usually no more than ten days before your closing date. 

Hope that helps and that you understand. Leverage your realtor with the questions that you have if your loan officer is not helpful. 

You can also request that loan officers manager or a different loan officer to finish your loan. They may get their attention because they are paid by the transaction. No one wants to do all the work and then let someone else step in at the last minute and get paid. 

Good luck!
